analysis.one_liner: Bars giant app stores from forcing developers to use their payment systems or blocking rival app stores.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill that cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2022 never received a Senate floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets companies that own app stores with more than 50 million U.S. users — in practice Apple and Google. It would stop them from forcing developers to use the store's own payment system, from punishing developers who offer cheaper prices elsewhere, from blocking users from installing rival app stores, and from ranking their own apps above competitors. The Federal Trade Commission, the Justice Department, state attorneys general, and developers could enforce the rules, and injured developers could recover triple damages.
analysis.who_benefits: App developers, who would no longer have to route sales through the store owner's payment system and give up a cut that has run up to 30%, and consumers, who could see lower app and service prices and more choice in where they get apps. Small developers and companies like Epic Games, Spotify, and Match Group pushed hard for this change.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits covered companies from requiring developers to use an in-app payment system owned by the store itself as a condition of distribution, which the bill frames as cutting gatekeeper costs that flow into prices.
Bars punitive action against developers who offer different pricing or payment options on other app stores or payment systems, so a developer's customers could learn about cheaper offers.

Requires companies controlling the operating system to let users install third-party apps and app stores through other means and set third-party stores as defaults, breaking the single-store bottleneck.
Bans using nonpublic business data collected from a third-party app to compete with it, and bans unreasonably ranking the store owner's own apps above rivals in search results.
Gives developers the right to sue for triple damages and gives the FTC, DOJ, and state attorneys general enforcement authority, so the rules do not depend on one agency alone.

analysis.who_pays: Apple and Google, whose app stores are the dominant way software reaches phone users and whose payment systems collect commissions on in-app sales. Losing mandatory payment routing and the single-store gate would put a large, recurring revenue stream at risk, and both would face new compliance and litigation costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Apple and Google's app store businesses

drawbacks.text: Critics, including Apple, argued that allowing third-party app stores and installs outside the official store would weaken privacy and security protections, exposing users to more malware and fraud; the bill includes a safety and privacy carve-out, but critics said its terms would invite years of litigation over what counts as 'necessary' protection.

Security exceptions only apply if the company proves by a preponderance of the evidence that protections are applied consistently, are not a pretext, and are narrowly tailored — a standard that puts every moderation and review decision at risk of becoming the subject of a lawsuit.
The bill applies only to app stores with more than 50 million U.S. users, so it regulates two companies by name in practice rather than setting a general rule for the market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: breaking the 30%-style commission and the single-store gate would very likely lower costs for developers and consumers, while opening the phone to outside software genuinely raises fraud and privacy risks that the bill's carve-out may not fully manage. The bill is aggressive but built with enforcement and reporting provisions to test its own effects after three years.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it on a bipartisan basis and put it on the Senate's calendar in February 2022, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the bill in August 2021 with cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Blackburn, Rubio, Lummis, Graham, Kennedy, and Hawley.
The Judiciary Committee ordered the bill favorably reported with an amendment in the nature of a substitute in February 2022.
On February 17, 2022 the committee reported the bill and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 275.
No further Senate action followed; the bill never reached a floor vote and died at the end of the 117th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Apple and Google, which keep their app store payment rules, their commission revenue, and their control over what software can reach phones — a system the bill was written to break up. The app developers who backed the bill got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Apple and Google's app store businesses

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Open App Markets Act and led it through introduction and committee consideration.

for.name: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.role: Republican cosponsors (Blackburn, Rubio, Lummis, Graham, Kennedy, Hawley, and one other)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan from introduction.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Democratic cosponsors (Klobuchar, Booker, Hirono, Durbin, and others)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill alongside its Democratic sponsor.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill favorably reported with an amendment in February 2022 and placed it on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Coalition for App Fairness and major app developers (Epic Games, Spotify, Match Group)
for.role: Industry coalition of developers opposing app store gatekeeping
for.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned for the bill, arguing Apple and Google's commissions and rules squeeze developers.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote after it was placed on the calendar in February 2022.

against.name: Apple
against.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily against the bill, arguing it would force iPhones to allow unsafe software and undermine privacy and security.

against.name: Google
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the bill, which would break its Play Store payment rules and sideloading restrictions.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction: 7 of 50 Senate Republicans and 7 of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsored it, and the Judiciary Committee reported it favorably; the obstacle was floor time, not party opposition.

industries.industry: Apple and Google (mobile app store gatekeepers)
industries.note: The bill would ban the rules that let them require developers to use their payment systems and pay commissions that have reached 30%, and would force open their phones to rival app stores. Their interest in keeping the gate runs against developers and consumers who pay higher prices as a result.

industries.industry: App developers, especially small and mid-sized developers
industries.note: Developers could use rival payment systems, tell users about cheaper prices, sue for triple damages if excluded, and avoid the store owner competing against them with their own data. Consumers share the benefit through lower prices and more choice.
With the store owner's payment system no longer mandatory, independent payment providers could compete for in-app transactions, a market the bill would open up.
